# Escalation

`customer_support.obj.core.escalation` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> A transfer of ownership, upward or sideways, with a reason and a NAMED RECEIVER. The named receiver is the whole definition: without one this is a complaint that has been logged loudly, and treating it as an escalation is how a queue reports an escalation rate it has not earned. Escalation is not a synonym for urgent, not a synonym for angry, and not a priority bump — all three can be true without a single unit of ownership moving. Customer-initiated and internally-triggered escalations are different animals requiring opposite responses. The first is a relationship event: something was promised, the promise broke, and the customer has stopped believing the current owner can fix it — the repair is mostly social and the technical work is secondary. The second is a process event: the current owner has correctly determined the problem exceeds their reach, and the repair is entirely logistical. Running a relationship event as a process event produces a technically flawless handoff to a customer who is already gone. The timing is unforgiving in both directions. Escalating early costs credibility — the receiver learns that this owner escalates rather than works, and the next one gets a slower answer. Escalating late costs the account. The window between those is short and nothing marks it, which is why `window_state` is a first-class property rather than a derived afterthought. The characteristic failure is escalating the ticket without escalating the CONTEXT: the receiver opens a case with a subject line and a severity, asks the customer what is going on, and the customer explains the same problem for the third time to a more senior person. That is worse than no escalation, because it converts seniority into evidence that nobody here is listening. And an escalation that bounces back down is worse still — it tells the customer that the escalation path itself does not work, and there is no second one.


Also called: `Manager Escalation`, `Tier Escalation`, `Executive Escalation`, `Raise`

## Preconditions

- **`esc.named_receiver_exists`** A named receiving owner must exist before an escalation can be created. _(unmet → block)_
- **`esc.ticket_actually_stuck`** The underlying work must genuinely be blocked or exhausted, not merely unfinished. _(unmet → degrade)_
- **`esc.entitlement_known`** Entitlement must be known before the receiver is put in a position to promise anything. _(unmet → degrade)_


## Constraints

- **`esc.no_escalation_without_named_receiver`** An escalation cannot exist without a named human receiver. A queue, a rota or a distribution list is not a receiver — none of them can accept ownership.
- **`esc.context_travels_with_ownership`** Ownership cannot transfer without the diagnosis, the history, and what was already promised.
- **`esc.one_owner_at_a_time`** Exactly one party owns the outcome at any moment. Two owners is zero owners, and it is the normal state of a swarm that was never given a lead.
- **`esc.cannot_promise_beyond_entitlement`** Nothing may be offered during an escalation that exceeds entitlement_ref, however senior the person offering it.
- **`esc.customer_must_not_learn_from_silence`** The customer must be told an escalation is underway. Internal acceptance is invisible to them and silence is indistinguishable from being ignored.
- **`esc.bounce_is_not_a_customer_communication`** A bounce must never be communicated to the customer as a routine reassignment. They will read it correctly either way; the only question is whether we said it first. _(soft)_
- **`esc.escalation_does_not_reset_the_clock`** Transferring ownership does not pause or restart the ticket's SLA. An escalation that resets its own clock is a queue-health illusion.


## Business rules

- **`esc.named_receiver_required`** An escalation with receiver_named false must not be recorded, reported or counted as an escalation. It is a complaint. Counting it inflates escalation rate, deflates time-to-acceptance, and hides the requests nobody picked up — which are the only ones that matter.

- **`esc.context_must_travel_with_ownership`** Ownership must not transfer while context_handed_over is false. The receiver inherits the customer's patience along with the ticket, and restarting the diagnosis spends it.

- **`esc.customer_must_be_told`** A customer-initiated escalation must be acknowledged to the customer before the internal transfer completes. Acceptance is invisible to them; silence is not.

- **`esc.bounce_requires_review`** An escalation returned to the previous owner must be reviewed by a human before the customer is told anything. A bounce is a failure of the escalation process and is almost never a fact about the ticket.

- **`esc.no_promise_beyond_entitlement`** No commitment made during an escalation may exceed entitlement_ref. Senior people settle rooms by promising things, and an out-of-entitlement promise made under pressure becomes the next escalation.

- **`esc.escalation_is_not_a_priority_bump`** Raising priority or severity without naming a receiver must not be recorded as an escalation. Priority is what we work on first; escalation is who owns it. Every ticketing product on the market conflates these and it is why escalation data is worthless.

- **`esc.thread_growth_is_reportable`** When the number of parties attached to the thread crosses a working-group size, the situation should be reviewed for incident status regardless of whether anyone declared one. Escalations grow the graph before anyone names what is happening.

- **`esc.repeat_escalation_outranks_severity`** A second escalation on the same account or issue must be handled above its assessed severity. The first escalation tested the fault; the second tests whether we have a process, and losing that test is not recoverable at the working level.



## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **An escalation may be legitimately refused when the ticket is simply not finished yet.** — Escalating unfinished work moves the queue rather than the problem, and it teaches the organisation that escalation is a way to skip diagnosis. Refusing needs to be a visible, explainable move rather than a silent non-response. _(overrides esc.named_receiver_required)_
- **When the trigger is relationship damage rather than technical difficulty, the correct receiver is the account owner and not a senior engineer.** — Customer-initiated escalations are relationship events. Routing one to deeper technical expertise answers a question nobody asked and usually adds a day.
- **An account that escalates routinely has destroyed the signal, and its escalations are read on severity rather than on the fact of escalation.** — The mechanism assumes escalation is costly to the customer. Where it is not, treating each one as high-signal starves every other account of attention — and the real finding is usually a mis-set expectation at sale.
- **A team may escalate before the customer asks, when the outcome is already known to be unacceptable.** — Waiting for the customer to demand a manager converts a recoverable situation into a relationship event. The best escalations are the ones the customer never had to request.
- **An executive-to-executive escalation may bypass the ladder entirely.** — It is a commercial conversation wearing a support ticket's clothing. Forcing it through tiers wastes everyone's time and the tiers cannot resolve what it is actually about.


## Best practices

- **Hand over a written statement of what was tried, what was ruled out, and what the customer has already been told.** — The characteristic failure is escalating the ticket without the context, so the receiver restarts a diagnosis the customer has already sat through twice. That repetition, not the delay, is what customers describe as the worst part.
- **Tell the customer the escalation occurred and name what changes because of it.** — A silent escalation gets no relationship credit at all. The customer experiences the same wait and concludes that asking for a manager achieved nothing, which is the opposite of the intended effect.
- **Raise it on the trajectory, not on the complaint.** — Escalating early costs credibility; escalating late costs the account. The window between is short and unmarked, and the only cheap way to stay inside it is to watch the trajectory rather than wait for the demand.
- **Return the outcome to the agent who escalated.** — Otherwise escalation is a place tickets disappear into, agents stop learning what they could have done, and the same escalation recurs.


## Anti-patterns

- **Using escalation to move a ticket up the queue rather than to transfer ownership.** — tempting because It works, it is faster than arguing about priority, and the two mechanisms look identical from the agent's side of the screen. Instead: Fix priority through triage; reserve escalation for genuine transfers of ownership.
- **Reassigning the ticket to a senior owner with no handover note.** — tempting because The history is 'all there in the ticket', and writing the summary takes longer than the reassignment. Instead: Require what-was-tried, what-was-ruled-out and what-the-customer-was-told before the transfer commits.
- **Escalating up and then bouncing the ticket back down when the receiver disagrees.** — tempting because Each hop is individually defensible — the receiver genuinely believes it belongs elsewhere. Instead: Treat a bounce as a reviewable event and fix the routing rule that produced it.
- **A senior receiver committing to something the contract does not cover, to make the escalation stop.** — tempting because It ends the immediate pain, the receiver has the authority, and nobody in the room is measured on the precedent. Instead: Check entitlement before the transfer commits, and route genuinely commercial asks to the account team.

- `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement` — requires (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.incident` — invalidated_by (hard)
- `customer_support.obj.core.churn_risk` — enriches (soft)


## Inputs

- **email** — who owes the next message
- **email** — last message received from the customer
- **derived** — observation balance as a sentiment proxy
- **derived** — number of parties attached to the thread
- **email** — overdue promises on the thread
- **ticket** — assignee changes, reopen count, escalation flags
- **phone** — the manager request, which is where it most often happens
- **chat** — escalation language in live conversation
- **crm** — account value, renewal date, named relationship owner
- **survey** — a detractor score arriving mid-ticket, which is an escalation nobody filed
- **manual_entry** — the reason and the context package, which no system infers


## Outputs

- **`escalation_confidence_bp`** How sure we are an escalation is forming or has formed. Precursor-weighted today, since nothing observes the act itself. → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker
- **`receiver_gap`** True when a transfer was requested and no named human has accepted. The single most actionable output on the object. → L4.decision_maker, L5.execution_planning
- **`context_package`** What must travel with the ownership. Emitted so the handoff can be assembled rather than remembered. → L5.execution_planning
- **`customer_acknowledgement_due`** True when the customer has not been told their escalation was received. Independent of internal progress and usually more urgent. → L5.communication_planning
- **`window_position`** too_early / in_window / late / missed. Consumed as a timing constraint, not a score. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`bounce_risk_bp`** Likelihood the receiver returns it. Reads context completeness and reason — a `wrong_owner` transfer with no context bounces almost by definition. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`notification_urgency`** How fast and by what channel the customer and the receiver must each be reached. They are rarely the same answer. → L5.2.channel_planner
- **`escalation_outcome_label`** Resolved / de-escalated / bounced / absorbed. Separated for Layer 6 because the four teach different lessons. → L6.learning_unit


## Events

- **`esc.requested`** Escalation Requested
- **`esc.receiver_named`** Receiver Named
- **`esc.accepted`** Escalation Accepted
- **`esc.context_gap_detected`** Context Did Not Travel
- **`esc.customer_waiting_again`** Customer Waiting On Us Again
- **`esc.window_opened`** Escalation Window Opened
- **`esc.bounced_back`** Escalation Bounced Back
- **`esc.de_escalated`** De-escalated By Agreement
- **`esc.thread_growing`** Parties Attaching To Thread


## Actions

- **Name a receiving owner** (human) — Converts a complaint into an escalation. Everything else on this object is downstream of it, and it costs one decision.
- **Assemble the context package** (agent) — Reproduction steps, what is ruled out, what the customer has already been told, and what was promised and by whom. The last of the four is the one most often missing and the most expensive to omit.
- **Tell the customer it has been escalated** (human) — Names who now owns it and by when they will make contact. A named person and a time; anything vaguer reads as a holding message and provokes the next escalation.
- **Do not escalate yet** (human) — The correct move in the too_early window: answer directly, keep ownership, and set a checkpoint. Escalating here teaches the receiver that this owner escalates rather than works, and the next escalation from them is slower.
- **Transfer ownership** (human) — Move ownership with the context attached. Should be blocked while context_handed_over is false — see esc.context_must_travel_with_ownership.
- **Brief the receiver before they contact the customer** (human) — Five minutes with the previous owner prevents the receiver contradicting a promise made before they arrived. The cheapest defence against the bounce, and almost never done.
- **Return ownership by agreement** (human) — Requires the customer's agreement, explicitly. Returning ownership without it is a bounce wearing the wrong label, and it will be recorded as a success.
- **Fold into a declared incident** (system) — Correct when several escalations share a cause. Reversible on purpose: an escalation absorbed into an incident that does not actually explain it ends up with no owner at all once the incident closes.
- **Tell whoever owns the relationship** (system) — Not the same as escalating. The account owner needs to know before the customer tells them, and being told by the customer is the thing that turns a support escalation into a commercial one.


## Evidence

- **ticket** · 9500 bp — An assignee change with a recorded reason and an acceptance timestamp. The closest thing to proof this object has — and it is unavailable today, which is the whole story of this file.
- **email** · 8000 bp — The customer asking in writing, or a receiver accepting in writing. Strong, and systematically biased toward second escalations: the first one usually happened on a call.
- **chat** · 7500 bp — Live escalation language. High strength, short retention, rarely searched.
- **phone** · 7000 bp — Where most customer-initiated escalations actually occur. Worth 7000 when captured and near zero in practice, because it is captured through a human writing it down afterwards.
- **meeting_transcript** · 7000 bp — An escalation raised in a QBR or a review call. Usually the highest-stakes kind and the least likely to be in the ticket.
- **crm** · 6000 bp — Account team records of a raised concern. Frequently the first place an executive escalation is visible.
- **survey** · 5500 bp — A detractor response mid-ticket. An escalation the customer filed with a scale instead of a sentence.
- **manual_entry** · 5000 bp — An agent logging it. Honest but self-reported, and agents under-report escalations they expect to be judged on.
- **derived** · 3500 bp — Inferred from sentiment, silence and thread growth. Every executable pattern on this object lands here. Corroborating only — never sole grounds for telling a manager a customer is escalating.


## Metrics

- **escalation_rate** (percent) — Share of tickets escalated. Uninterpretable unless receiver_named gates the count — otherwise it measures how freely people use a flag.
- **time_to_named_receiver** (hours) — Request to a named human. Distinct from time to acceptance, and the one the customer feels.
- **time_to_acceptance** (hours) — Request to ownership genuinely moving. The internal health measure of the escalation path.
- **bounce_back_rate** (percent) — Share returned to the previous owner. The best single indicator that the escalation process is decorative.
- **context_completeness_at_handoff** (percent) — Share of transfers where the receiver did not have to re-diagnose. Requires diagnosis_repeats, which nothing records today.
- **repeat_escalation_rate** (percent) — Second escalations on the same account or issue. Measures whether the first one worked, which escalation_rate cannot.
- **de_escalation_rate** (percent) — Share returned to the normal path by agreement. Must be reported separately from bounces or it flatters the exact failure it should expose.
- **post_escalation_retention** (percent) — Whether accounts that escalated stayed. The only metric here that measures the point of the exercise.
- **customer_wait_after_escalation** (hours) — Time with ball_in_court on us after a transfer. Computable today from live facts, unlike everything above it.

## Examples

- **Customer asks for a manager on a call, third contact on the same bug** — origin customer_initiated, reason repeat_contact. A relationship event: the technical fix is necessary and will not settle it. If it is handled as a routing problem the manager arrives, asks what happened, and confirms the customer's suspicion that nobody has been listening.
- **Agent hands a database corruption case to engineering** — origin agent_initiated, direction sideways, reason technical_depth. A process event and the healthiest kind — correctly recognising the limit of your reach is what tiering is for. Fails only on context: engineering restarts the diagnosis unless the package travels.
- **Escalated to a tier-2 owner who returns it two days later saying it is a config question** — outcome bounced_back, bounce_count 1. Worse than never escalating. The customer waited two days to be handed back to the person they had already given up on, and the escalation path has now been discredited in front of them.
- **An SLA clock breaches overnight and an auto-escalation fires into an empty rota** — origin system_triggered, receiver_named false. Not an escalation. It is an alert, and counting it makes the escalation dashboard report a functioning process at exactly the moment there is nobody on the other end.
- **Customer emails the CEO after two weeks of no update** — origin customer_initiated, executive_visible true, credibility_cost severe. The window was missed a long way back — probably at the first broken commitment. Everything from here is damage control and the reporting obligation outlives the ticket.
- **Agent escalates within twenty minutes of first contact because the customer sounded annoyed** — window_state too_early. The receiver learns this agent escalates rather than works, and the next one — which will be real — gets a slower answer. The cost is invisible, deferred, and paid by a different customer.
- **Nine escalations in an afternoon, all pointing at the same failed deploy** — Should be merged into an incident, and the merge is almost always recognised late. Nine separately owned escalations produce nine slightly different stories reaching nine customers.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> Twelve inference patterns: four executable, eight needs_signal. Every executable one is a PRECURSOR pattern reading generic relationship telemetry — a broken commitment nobody answered for, an objection left past this customer's own reply cadence, sentiment turning while we hold the ball, a thread quietly acquiring people. None of them observe an escalation, because nothing in the substrate can. That is the correct trade: the precursors fire while the situation is still cheap to fix, and by the time an escalation is declared the credibility is already spent. The two highest-value Layer 2 asks this object generates are `escalation_requested` and `escalation_accepted`. The first is unusually tractable — the phrasing is stereotyped in every language support runs in. The second is the more important of the pair: without it there is no machine-checkable difference between an escalation and a complaint, and escalation rate remains a number that measures how freely people click a button. `ticket.reopen_count` is the cheapest strong predictor in the domain and needs no language model at all; it is a counter, and its absence is why this brain cannot currently tell a first contact from a fourth.
